How do Parties vote in the Austrian National Council? Part II

Austria
parliament
ParlAT

A follow-up that traces how parties shift their position on a government bill (Regierungsvorlage) as it moves through committee, the second reading and the third reading in the Austrian National Council — and asks where, if anywhere, those changes actually happen.

Author

Roland Schmidt

Published

8 Jun 2026

Modified

20 Aug 2026

Just the results, please

1 Context

In Part I of this post, I showcased how the {ParlAT} package offers some simple, yet powerful means to analyze voting behavior of parties in the Austrian National Council. The analysis detailed how parties voted (for or against) and on the frequency of party-combinations, i.e. how often e.g. party A voted with party B. All of the presented analysis dealt with the votes in the third reading, that is, at the last stage of the legislative procedure in the National Council.

In this post I want to expand the analysis beyond the third reading and include the earlier stages of the legislative process in the National Council as well: the committee (Ausschuss), the second reading and the third reading. While doing this my interest is not so much how a party voted at a specific stage, but more on whether and how often party positions on a legislative item actually changed over the course of the different stages within the National Council. With this general interest a number of other questions lend themselves to being answered:

  • between which stages (committee → second reading, second → third reading) do the most changes happen?
  • how do parties differ when it comes to the frequency of changing their voting position over the course of different stages?
  • during which government can we observe most vote changes?

On a conceptual level, I believe that answering these questions can contribute to a better understanding of how government parties respond to opposition demands. Strictly speaking, a change of vote could also simply mean that an opposition party changed its mind after further consideration. While that is possible, it is unlikely; in most cases a change of an opposition party’s vote means that the party got something in return. Whether this was indeed a change in the content of the bill at stake, or on another, unrelated issue, can’t be answered without looking into the details of the specific item. But retrieving these numbers is a first step.

Two conceptual notes of caution:

  • Absolute numbers can mislead. For a flip from no to yes to materialize we need to have a ‘no’ in the first place. If there never was a ‘no’, i.e. if a bill enjoyed unanimous support from the start, there cannot be any flip either. But in that case, the absence of a flip obviously does not indicate a lack of government responsiveness.
  • Legislative periods aren’t directly comparable. Different legislative periods have different legislative items at play, and these may vary in their level of contestation, i.e. how difficult it is for government and opposition parties to find common ground. Not every legislative period brings up items of similar levels of contestation.

2 Set-up

Get the necessary packages. In addition, I define here a small helper function which gives all reactable tables in this post a consistent look (title, optional subtitle, and a source note at the bottom), so I don’t have to repeat the same styling code over and over again.

Load packages 
library(ParlAT)
library(tidyverse)
library(furrr)
library(reactable)
library(reactablefmtr)
library(naniar)
library(ggtext)

# shared table theme and attribution footer for all reactable tables
compact_table_theme <- reactablefmtr::fivethirtyeight(font_size = 12)
table_source <- reactablefmtr::html(
  "<span style='font-size:8pt;color:grey30;font-family:Segoe UI !important;line-height:0.5'>Source: www.parlament.gv.at. Analysis: Roland Schmidt - @zoowalk.bsky.social - https://werk.statt.codes</span>"
)

# helper that wraps any reactable with a consistent title, optional subtitle, and source footer
style_reactable_table <- function(table, title, subtitle = NULL) {
  styled_table <- table %>%
    reactablefmtr::add_title(
      title = reactablefmtr::html(paste0(
        "<span style='font-size:12pt;'>",
        title,
        "</span>"
      ))
    )

  if (!is.null(subtitle)) {
    styled_table <- styled_table %>%
      reactablefmtr::add_subtitle(
        subtitle = reactablefmtr::html(paste0(
          "<span style='font-size:10pt;line-height:0.5;'>",
          subtitle,
          "</span>"
        )),
        font_color = "grey30",
        font_weight = "normal",
        font_style = "italic"
      )
  }

  styled_table %>%
    reactablefmtr::add_source(source = table_source)
}

3 Get Data

3.1 Data on the readings

This section assembles the first half of the dataset: the bills themselves and the stage data recorded on their own pages, which is where the second- and third-reading votes live. The other half — the committee vote, which as we’ll see is not recorded there — follows in the next section, and the two are brought together after that.

3.1.1 Query the items

As in the previous post, let’s start by getting the government bills (‘Regierungsvorlagen’) of the National Council for the legislative periods 20 to 28. With {ParlAT}.

Fetch National Council government bills and cache them 
# fetch RV (Regierungsvorlagen) for legislative periods 20–28 (GP XX through XXVIII)
items_20_28 <- seq(20, 28) %>%
  map(., \(x) get_items(item = "RV", legis_period = x, institution = "NR")) %>%
  list_rbind() # stack per-period tibbles into one dataframe

# guard against overwriting a good cache with an empty/failed fetch
if (nrow(items_20_28) == 0) {
  stop("The RV fetch returned no rows; the existing items cache was not overwritten.")
}

readr::write_rds(
  items_20_28,
  here::here(
    "posts",
    "2026-06-08-ParlAT-votingPatterns-2",
    "_data",
    "items_20_28.rds"
  )
)
Code 
nrow(items_20_28)
## [1] 2710

3.1.2 Query the stages

Now let’s feed the URLs of the obtained items to get_item_details(), this time with the stages parameter set to TRUE. The stages data contains one row per procedural step of an item, and — crucially for this post — the description of each voting step. As in the previous post, I wrap the function call in purrr’s safely() to collect any potential errors without breaking the loop, and use future_map() to query the API with multiple workers simultaneously, i.e. to speed up the process.

Fetch item details with stages and cache them 
plan(multisession, workers = 4) # parallelise across 4 cores to speed up API fetching

item_urls <- items_20_28 %>%
  pull(item_url)

# wrap in safely() so a single failed request returns an error slot instead of halting the loop
safe_get_item_details <- safely(get_item_details)

item_details_raw <- item_urls %>%
  future_map(
    \(x) {
      safe_result <- safe_get_item_details(item_url = x, stages = TRUE)
      safe_result$item_url <- x # attach URL so failed results can be identified later
      safe_result
    },
    .progress = TRUE,
    .options = furrr_options(packages = c("ParlAT", "purrr", "tibble"))
  )

plan(sequential) # reset to single-threaded after parallel fetch

# don't overwrite a good cache if every request failed
item_success_n <- sum(map_lgl(item_details_raw, \(x) is.null(x$error)))
if (item_success_n == 0) {
  stop(paste0(
    "All ", length(item_details_raw),
    " item-detail requests failed; the existing cache was not overwritten. ",
    "First error: ", conditionMessage(item_details_raw[[1]]$error)
  ))
}

# persist the raw fetch results so re-renders don't need to re-hit the API
readr::write_rds(
  item_details_raw,
  here::here(
    "posts",
    "2026-06-08-ParlAT-votingPatterns-2",
    "_data",
    "item_details_raw.rds"
  )
)

3.1.3 Prepare stages data

Below, I a) check for any failed calls, and b) combine the successful calls into a single data frame. Subsequently, I unnest the stages column so that we get one row per procedural step per item. Note that at this point the data frame still contains all stage rows for each item — also those without any vote. Filtering for the actual votes comes next.

Combine successful fetches and unnest stages into one row per step 
# collect items where the API call failed; conditionMessage() extracts the error string
failed_items <- item_details_raw |>
  keep(\(x) !is.null(x$error)) |>
  map(\(x) tibble(item_url = x$item_url, error = conditionMessage(x$error))) |>
  list_rbind()
failed_items
## data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows

# keep only successful results and extract the nested $result element
item_details <- item_details_raw |>
  keep(\(x) is.null(x$error)) |>
  map("result") |>
  list_rbind()

# unnest stages into one row per stage per item
item_stages <- item_details |>
  select(
    item_url,
    legis_period,
    type_doc,
    title,
    item_number,
    status_number,
    status_description,
    stages
  ) |>
  filter(map_lgl(stages, \(x) !is.null(x))) |> # drop items with no stage data at all
  unnest(stages) %>%
  mutate(stage_date = lubridate::dmy(stage_date))

# used in inline text and table subtitles throughout the document.
# Two guards: na.rm, because a single unparseable date would otherwise render every
# "Data as of ..." line as "NA"; and the cap at today's date, because the stages table
# also carries *scheduled* future sittings. Taking a plain maximum would date the whole
# post weeks ahead of the last vote actually recorded in it.
data_cutoff <- max(
  item_stages$stage_date[item_stages$stage_date <= Sys.Date()],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

The screenshot in the margin is from the website of the Parliament and shows the details on the different stages of one specific bill — the same kind of information we just retrieved with the code chunk above. Two things are worth flagging up front. First, at this point we have data on all stages, not only voting results; rows we’re not interested in still need to be dropped. Second, and this is something what we have to take care off further below, the stage data does not contain any info on the committee’s own vote — that lives in a different entry, the one belonging to the committee’s report on the bill.

To make this concrete, the example below follows one specific bill end to end, through every transformation step in this post: a 2024 amendment to the Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz (the renewable-energy-expansion act). It’s a good running example precisely because it isn’t a straightforward case: the FPÖ moves from opposing it in committee to supporting it by the second reading, and the SPÖ opposes it through the second reading before coming around at the third — so we’ll be able to watch both kinds of position change appear in the data as the pipeline builds up. Querying the bill’s own page with get_item_details(stages = TRUE) returns the stages shown in the screenshot and table below.

# the one bill this post follows end to end through every transformation step below
example_item_url <- "https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608"

item_stages_example <- get_item_details(item_url = example_item_url, stages = TRUE) %>%
  select(
    item_url,
    legis_period,
    type_doc,
    stages,
    title,
    item_number,
    status_number,
    status_description
  ) |>
  filter(map_lgl(stages, \(x) !is.null(x))) |> # drop items with no stage data at all
  unnest(stages) %>%
  mutate(stage_date = lubridate::dmy(stage_date)) %>%
  select(phase, stage_name, stage_date, item_url)
item_stages_example

As you can see in the output above, each row is identical to the rows presented on the item’s detail page on the website of the Austrian Parliament. From these rows we will later keep only the rows containing relevant votes for the second and third reading; and subsequently extract from these rows the voting decisions for each individual party. Contrasting the obtained results between the different readings allows identifying whether a party changed its position over the course of the legislative proceedings in the National Council.

3.2 Committee reports

While we have now all available data which is included in the stage data of a legislative item, it turns out that there is a gap on the votes casted in the committees. It is worth pausing on what the item’s own page records about its committee phase, because, as it turns out, surprisingly little of it is the actual vote. A committee does far more than decide on a bill: it requests written opinions (Stellungnahmen), sets deadlines (Fristsetzungen), refers items back, and so on. The table below breaks all of a bill’s National Council committee stages down by type. The conclusion: the formal adoption vote, the committee’s decision on the bill, the part we actually want, appears on the bill’s own page only rarely. That is exactly why the rest of this section goes after the committee reports and takes the committee vote from there instead.

Categorise National Council committee stages and show the vote share 
# same vote-keyword set the scope filter below relies on
committee_vote_keywords <- "dafür|wechselnde Mehrheit|getrennte Abstimmung|namentliche Abstimmung|abgelehnt|mehrstimmig"

# classify every National Council committee stage by what it records
committee_stages <- item_stages %>%
  filter(phase == "Ausschussberatungen NR") %>%
  mutate(
    is_vote = str_detect(
      stage_name,
      regex(committee_vote_keywords, ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    category = case_when(
      str_detect(
        stage_name,
        regex("Antrag auf Annahme des", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ) ~ "Adoption vote on the bill",
      str_detect(
        stage_name,
        regex("Einholung einer Stellungnahme", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ) ~ "Opinion request (Stellungnahme)",
      str_detect(stage_name, regex("Fristsetzung", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~
        "Deadline motion (Fristsetzung)",
      is_vote ~ "Other vote",
      .default = "Non-vote / procedural"
    ),
    # flags the committee's formal adoption vote. Note this is *not* the row that reaches
    # the analysis: the committee position is taken from the committee report instead
    # (see below), because the bill's own page records the adoption vote only rarely
    is_adoption_vote = category == "Adoption vote on the bill"
  )

# aggregate to one row per category with its share of all committee stages
committee_category_summary <- committee_stages %>%
  summarise(rows = n(), .by = c(category, is_adoption_vote)) %>%
  mutate(
    share = rows / sum(rows),
    is_adoption_vote_label = if_else(is_adoption_vote, "Yes", "No")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(rows)) %>%
  select(category, rows, share, is_adoption_vote_label)

committee_category_table <- reactable(
  committee_category_summary,
  columns = list(
    category = colDef(name = "Committee stage type", minWidth = 230),
    rows = colDef(
      name = "Stages",
      align = "right",
      minWidth = 90,
      format = colFormat(separators = TRUE)
    ),
    share = colDef(
      name = "Share of committee stages",
      minWidth = 230,
      align = "left",
      # data bars make the tiny vote share read at a glance against the procedural bulk
      cell = reactablefmtr::data_bars(
        committee_category_summary,
        max_value = 1,
        number_fmt = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1),
        fill_color = "#1a9641",
        background = "#f0f0f0",
        text_position = "outside-end"
      )
    ),
    is_adoption_vote_label = colDef(
      name = "Adoption vote?",
      align = "center",
      minWidth = 130
    )
  ),
  fullWidth = TRUE,
  compact = TRUE,
  highlight = TRUE,
  outlined = TRUE,
  theme = compact_table_theme
) %>%
  style_reactable_table(
    "WHAT THE BILL'S OWN PAGE RECORDS ABOUT ITS COMMITTEE PHASE",
    paste0(
      "All committee stages recorded on the bills' own pages, by type — the adoption vote is the rarest of them. Data as of ",
      data_cutoff,
      "."
    )
  )

committee_category_table

Across all 10,438 committee stages recorded on the bills’ own pages, only 0.9% record a vote at all, and just 0.4% are the bill-adoption vote — which is why the committee position is taken from the committee report rather than from these rows.

3.2.1 Linking a report to its bill

To demonstrate how to get the committee voting data, let’s now fetch the example bill’s companion report page the same way, with get_item_details(), and look at what it carries. Besides stages, every item, bill or report alike, also carries a references column: a list of typed cross-references to other legislative objects. That column is the mechanism to link a committee vote back to its bill.

Fetch the committee report’s own page and show its references, incl. the Hauptgegenstand (HG) link back to the bill 
example_report_url <- "https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2666"

item_report_example <- get_item_details(
  item_url = example_report_url,
  stages = TRUE
)

item_references_example <- item_report_example %>%
  select(references) %>%
  unnest(references) %>%
  select(text, subject, zitation, url, art)
item_references_example
## # A tibble: 1 × 5
##   text                         subject                              zitation  url                      art  
##   <chr>                        <chr>                                <chr>     <chr>                    <chr>
## 1 Hauptgegenstand des Berichts Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz, Änderung 2608 d.B. /gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608 HG
Code 
# resolve the HG row's relative url into the same absolute form item_url uses elsewhere
hg_parent_url <- item_references_example %>%
  filter(art == "HG") %>%
  mutate(parent_url = paste0("https://www.parlament.gv.at", url)) %>%
  pull(parent_url)

hg_parent_url
## [1] "https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608"

The report carries a single reference row here, typed HG. Its url resolves to https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608 — exactly the item_url of the bill’s own stages table shown further above. That one row is the entire link between the two datasets: a committee report holds no bill-specific vote information anywhere else, and a bill’s own page holds no back-reference to its report at all. art is how the Parliament’s data model types these cross-references; besides HG, a report can also carry MG (‘Mitgegenstand’, a co-subject bundled into the same report) and, more rarely, HGS, ZU or B for other bundling or referral cases — but only HG is used as the match key below.

3.2.2 Fetch the committee reports

With the link understood, we can go and get the reports themselves. The object holding the committee’s adoption vote is the committee report (Ausschussbericht, type AUB): it carries the formal Antrag auf Annahme des Gesetzesvorschlags section (the motion to adopt the bill), which includes each party’s vote, plus the HG reference back to the parent bill we just followed. So to capture committee votes properly, I fetch every committee report for periods 20–28 with its own targeted get_items() call, again with stages = TRUE.

Fetch all committee reports (Ausschussbericht) with stages and cache them 
aub_urls <- seq(20, 28) %>%
  map(., \(x) get_items(item = "AUB", legis_period = x, institution = "NR")) %>%
  list_rbind() %>%
  pull(item_url) %>%
  unique()

plan(multisession, workers = 4)
safe_get_item_details <- safely(get_item_details)

aub_details_raw <- aub_urls %>%
  future_map(
    \(x) {
      safe_result <- safe_get_item_details(item_url = x, stages = TRUE)
      safe_result$item_url <- x
      safe_result
    },
    .progress = TRUE,
    .options = furrr_options(packages = c("ParlAT", "purrr", "tibble"))
  )

plan(sequential)

aub_success_n <- sum(map_lgl(aub_details_raw, \(x) is.null(x$error)))
if (aub_success_n == 0) {
  stop(paste0(
    "All ", length(aub_details_raw),
    " committee-report requests failed; the existing AUB cache was not overwritten. ",
    "First error: ", conditionMessage(aub_details_raw[[1]]$error)
  ))
}

readr::write_rds(
  aub_details_raw,
  here::here("posts", "2026-06-08-ParlAT-votingPatterns-2", "_data", "aub_details_raw.rds")
)

3.2.3 Build committee votes from the reports

Now I turn the committee reports into usable committee votes. For each report I do two things: a) read its stages and keep the row whose stage_name matches Antrag auf Annahme des Gesetzesvorschlags (which holds the Dafür/Dagegen party split — the actual vote), and b) resolve its references to find the row typed HG and follow that row’s url back to the parent bill, exactly as demonstrated above for XXVII/I/2666. That HG reference is the only link between a report and its bill anywhere in the data: there’s no shared numeric ID between the two pages, and titles aren’t guaranteed to match character-for-character either (reports sometimes shorten or reformat a bill’s title), so references$url is the one connection actually worth trusting. The result is one committee-vote row per bill, carrying the parent bill’s identifiers so it slots in alongside the second- and third-reading rows further down.

Three places let rows silently drop out of this link — filter() and inner_join() don’t warn when they discard rows, so it’s worth being explicit about all of them:

  • No resolvable HG reference. A handful of reports have no references at all, or none typed HG — aub_parent’s map_chr() returns NA for these, and aub_committee_stages drops them via filter(!is.na(parent_url)).
  • The resolved parent isn’t one of our own bills. Even once a report resolves an HG url, that url has to match an item_url already present in parent_meta — i.e. a bill we actually fetched at the very start of this post. committee_rows’s inner_join(parent_meta, ...) drops any report whose parent isn’t found there — for instance a report belonging to a non-RV item, which falls outside this post’s scope.
  • The bill was bundled into another bill’s report as a co-subject. A few hundred reports carry MG (‘Mitgegenstand’) references alongside their HG. A bill that appears only as somebody else’s MG never resolves as an HG parent, so it gets no committee row at all — its committee vote was taken as part of a bundle rather than on its own. I don’t try to recover these.

One simplification is worth naming as well: a small number of reports (22 in the current data) carry more than one HG reference, i.e. they adopt several main subjects at once. hg$url[1] takes the first, so the committee vote is attributed to just one of them. Fixing this properly would mean fanning the report’s vote out across every HG it names; given how few reports are affected I’ve left the simplification in place, but it is a simplification, not a non-issue.

Extract committee votes from reports and link them to the parent bill 
# successful report fetches; retain the requested URL if an older cached result
# does not yet include the normalised item_url column
aub_details <- aub_details_raw |>
  keep(\(x) is.null(x$error)) |>
  map(\(x) {
    result <- x$result
    if (!"item_url" %in% names(result)) {
      result$item_url <- x$item_url
    }
    result
  }) |>
  list_rbind()

# link each report to its parent bill via the reference flagged "HG" (Hauptgegenstand)
aub_parent <- aub_details |>
  transmute(
    aub_url = item_url,
    parent_url = map_chr(references, \(r) {
      if (is.null(r) || !is.data.frame(r) || nrow(r) == 0) {
        return(NA_character_)
      }
      hg <- r[!is.na(r$art) & r$art == "HG", , drop = FALSE]
      if (nrow(hg) == 0) {
        return(NA_character_)
      }
      # [1]: a handful of reports adopt several main subjects at once and carry multiple HG
      # rows; this attributes the vote to the first of them (see the caveat above)
      paste0("https://www.parlament.gv.at", hg$url[1])
    })
  )

# the committee's adoption-vote stage(s) from each report, linked to the parent bill
aub_committee_stages <- aub_details |>
  select(aub_url = item_url, stages) |>
  filter(map_lgl(stages, \(x) !is.null(x))) |>
  unnest(stages) |>
  filter(str_detect(
    stage_name,
    regex("Antrag auf Annahme des", ignore_case = TRUE)
  )) |>
  mutate(stage_date = lubridate::dmy(stage_date)) |>
  left_join(aub_parent, by = "aub_url") |>
  filter(!is.na(parent_url))

# parent bill's item-level fields, so committee rows line up with the reading rows.
# Sourced from item_details rather than item_stages: a bill that returned no stage data
# is absent from item_stages and would silently lose its committee vote, even though it
# is in scope. (No bill is affected in the current data, but the join key should not
# depend on the bill happening to have stage rows.)
parent_meta <- item_details |>
  distinct(
    item_url,
    legis_period,
    type_doc,
    title,
    item_number,
    status_number,
    status_description
  )

# one committee row per bill (keep the latest adoption vote if a report has several)
committee_rows <- aub_committee_stages |>
  inner_join(parent_meta, by = c("parent_url" = "item_url")) |>
  transmute(
    item_url = parent_url,
    legis_period,
    type_doc,
    title,
    item_number,
    status_number,
    status_description,
    stage_date,
    stage_name,
    phase = "Ausschussbericht",
    reading = "committee"
  ) |>
  slice_max(stage_date, n = 1, by = item_url, with_ties = FALSE)

nrow(committee_rows) # committee votes available to merge with the readings
## [1] 2571

Here’s what that produces for our running example: a single committee-vote row for XXVII/I/2608, carrying the adoption-vote text straight from its report — the Dagegen list on this row is exactly where the FPÖ’s committee-stage opposition (before it flips at the second reading) comes from.

Show the committee vote row retrieved for the example item 
example_committee_row <- committee_rows %>%
  filter(item_url == example_item_url)
glimpse(example_committee_row)
## Rows: 1
## Columns: 11
## $ item_url           <chr> "https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/I/2608"

## $ type_doc           <chr> "RV"
## $ title              <chr> "Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz, Änderung"

## $ stage_name         <chr> "Ausschuss für Wirtschaft, Industrie und Energie: Antrag auf Annahme des unveränderten Gesetzesvorschlags\nDafür: ÖVP, GRÜNE, dagegen: SPÖ, FPÖ, NEOS"
## $ phase              <chr> "Ausschussbericht"

3.3 Combine committee votes with the readings

The committee votes are ready, one clean row per bill. The reading votes are not: the stage data fetched back in Data on the readings still holds every procedural step, votes and non-votes alike. So this section does two things — narrow that stage data down to the actual reading votes, and then bind the two sides together into the finalized dataset the rest of this post analyzes.

3.3.1 Scope the ordinary readings

First the narrowing. I reduce the bills’ own second- and third-reading stages down to just the rows where a vote was actually cast — a finished, vote-rows-only dataset for the “ordinary” readings. Along the way a reading column is added, recording the stage: second or third reading (or, in some cases, second and third at once). A second column, vote_report_type, is added one step later, once the committee rows have been bound on, since it applies to both sides alike.

Note that this filter keeps only stages whose description actually carries vote-outcome text. That is a substantial cut — a large majority of the discarded rows are entries like ‘NN. Sitzung des Nationalrates: Zweite und dritte Lesung’ which record that the readings happened but report no outcome at all, so there is nothing to extract a party position from.

Filter to NR readings and vote-outcome text — the ordinary, committee-free dataset 
items_scope_ordinary <- item_stages |>
  filter(str_detect(phase, regex("NR"))) %>% # keep only National Council (NR) phases
  # plenary 2nd/3rd readings from the bill's own stages
  # r? makes the pattern match both "zweite"/"zweiter" and "dritte"/"dritter".
  # ignore_case is required: stage names capitalise the ordinal after a colon, e.g.
  # "141. Sitzung des Nationalrates: Zweite Lesung", and those rows are real readings.
  filter(str_detect(stage_name, regex("(dritter?|zweiter?) Lesung", ignore_case = TRUE))) %>%
  mutate(
    reading = case_when(
      # some items combine both readings into a single stage entry.
      # these patterns must be case-insensitive for the same reason as the filter above —
      # otherwise "Zweite und dritte Lesung" would fall through to the "dritte" branch
      str_detect(stage_name, regex("zweite", ignore_case = TRUE)) &
        str_detect(stage_name, regex("dritte", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "second & third",
      str_detect(stage_name, regex("zweite", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "second",
      str_detect(stage_name, regex("dritte", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "third",
      .default = NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  # keep only stages that contain actual vote-outcome text — this is now a finished,
  # vote-rows-only dataset for the ordinary (non-committee) readings.
  # same keyword set defined once further above, reused here rather than re-typed
  filter(str_detect(
    stage_name,
    regex(committee_vote_keywords, ignore_case = TRUE)
  ))

nrow(items_scope_ordinary) # finished, committee-free vote dataset
## [1] 5221

For our running example, items_scope_ordinary now holds exactly the second- and third-reading rows — nothing else, and no committee row yet.

Show the example item’s rows in the finished, committee-free vote dataset 
example_vote_rows_ordinary <- items_scope_ordinary %>%
  filter(item_url == example_item_url) %>%
  select(title, stage_date, reading, stage_name)
example_vote_rows_ordinary
## # A tibble: 2 × 4
##   title                                stage_date reading stage_name                                                                                                                  
##   <chr>                                <date>     <chr>   <chr>                                                                                                                       
## 1 Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz, Änderung 2024-07-04 second  "272. Sitzung des Nationalrates: Gesetzesvorschlag in zweiter Lesung angenommen\nDafür: ÖVP, FPÖ, GRÜNE, dagegen: SPÖ, NEOS"
## 2 Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz, Änderung 2024-07-04 third   "272. Sitzung des Nationalrates: Gesetzesvorschlag in dritter Lesung angenommen\nDafür: ÖVP, SPÖ, FPÖ, GRÜNE, dagegen: NEOS"

3.3.2 Bind on the committee votes

Now the merge. committee_rows is already vote-rows-only by construction (see Build committee votes from the reports above — only the adoption-vote stage was ever kept), and items_scope_ordinary has just been reduced to vote rows too. The committee step is the bill’s first formal vote, taken before it reaches the plenary floor; including it lets us follow an item across three stages instead of two. vote_report_type is classified on the combined table, giving items_scope — the combined set of vote rows. Two cleaning steps still follow below: items with duplicated stage rows are dropped, and the analysis then keeps only the regular vote-report type (the one whose text lists parties explicitly, and so the only one a party-level position can be read from).

Bind on committee votes and classify vote report type 
items_scope <- items_scope_ordinary %>%
  bind_rows(committee_rows) %>%
  mutate(
    # classify how the vote result is reported; order matters — "regular" must come first
    # because some stage names contain both "dafür" and other keywords
    vote_report_type = case_when(
      # "regular" requires the explicit Dafür:/Dagegen: party-list separator the parser
      # keys on; parenthetical forms like "mehrstimmig (dafür S,V dagegen F)" fall through.
      # note "dafür:" *with* the colon: fn_get_votes() errors out on any row lacking it,
      # so the classifier has to guarantee that precondition rather than merely happen to
      str_detect(stage_name, regex("dafür:", ignore_case = TRUE)) &
        str_detect(stage_name, regex("dagegen", ignore_case = TRUE)) &
        str_detect(
          stage_name,
          regex(",\\s*dagegen:|\\.\\s*Dagegen:", ignore_case = TRUE)
        ) ~ "regular",
      str_detect(
        stage_name,
        regex("wechselnde Mehrheit", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ) ~ "wechselnde Mehrheit",
      str_detect(
        stage_name,
        regex("namentliche Abstimmung", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ) ~ "namentliche Abstimmung",
      str_detect(
        stage_name,
        regex("getrennte Abstimmung", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ) ~ "getrennte Abstimmung",
      str_detect(stage_name, regex("abgelehnt", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "abgelehnt",
      str_detect(
        stage_name,
        regex("mehrstimmig", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ) ~ "mehrstimmig",
      .default = NA
    )
  )

nrow(items_scope) # vote rows after binding committee votes onto the readings
## [1] 7792
nrow(item_stages) # for comparison: all stage rows, votes and non-votes alike
## [1] 67252

And here’s the payoff for our running example: the finalized, merged view — committee, second and third reading side by side for the same bill.

Show the example item’s rows in the finalized, merged dataset 
example_vote_rows_combined <- items_scope %>%
  filter(item_url == example_item_url) %>%
  select(reading, stage_date, vote_report_type, stage_name) %>%
  arrange(factor(reading, levels = c("committee", "second", "third")))
example_vote_rows_combined

3.3.3 Check for duplicate stage rows

Time for a data sanity check. Now that the analysis spans up to three stages — committee, second reading and third reading — an item no longer needs to have a fixed number of rows. What it should have, however, is at most one row per stage: a single committee vote, a single second-reading vote, a single third-reading vote. Any item with more than one row for the same stage points to a data inconsistency (duplicates in the source, or an item that was approved/rejected twice within one stage). Let’s see how many such cases there are.

Identify items with duplicate vote rows within a stage 
# each item should have at most one row per stage (committee / second / third)
dup_rows <- items_scope %>%
  count(legis_period, item_url, reading, name = "n_rows") %>%
  filter(n_rows > 1) # flag any item+stage combination that occurs more than once
n_distinct(dup_rows$item_url)
## [1] 9

There are 9 items out of 2608 which feature more than one row for the same stage.

To facilitate a closer look at these cases, the table below lists the affected items with their individual vote-stage rows. Each item is linked to its page on the parliament’s website, so you can check the underlying records yourself.

Build reactable table of items with duplicate vote rows in a stage 
# limit to only the offending items so the table stays focused.
# deliberately no distinct() here: where the source reports the same vote twice, those
# identical rows *are* the finding, and collapsing them would both hide the duplicate and
# make n_obs disagree with the n_rows count that flagged the item in the first place
non_pairs_details <- items_scope %>%
  semi_join(dup_rows, by = c("legis_period", "item_url")) %>%
  select(
    legis_period,
    item_url,
    stage_date,
    stage_name,
    vote_report_type
  ) %>%
  mutate(n_obs = n(), .by = c("legis_period", "item_url"))

non_pairs_details_display <- non_pairs_details %>%
  arrange(desc(n_obs), legis_period, item_url, stage_date) %>%
  mutate(
    # strip the base URL and query string to get a compact "XXVIII/I/403" style reference
    item_ref = item_url %>%
      str_remove("^https://www\\.parlament\\.gv\\.at/gegenstand/") %>%
      str_remove("\\?.*$")
  ) %>%
  select(
    legis_period,
    item_ref,
    stage_date,
    stage_name,
    vote_report_type,
    n_obs,
    item_url
  )

non_pairs_details_table <- reactable(
  non_pairs_details_display,
  columns = list(
    legis_period = colDef(
      name = "Legis. period",
      align = "right",
      minWidth = 90,
      filterable = TRUE
    ),
    item_ref = colDef(
      name = "Item",
      minWidth = 125,
      filterable = TRUE,
      # custom cell renderer turns the short reference into a clickable link
      cell = function(value, index) {
        htmltools::tags$a(
          href = non_pairs_details_display$item_url[index],
          target = "_blank",
          value
        )
      }
    ),
    stage_date = colDef(
      name = "Stage date",
      align = "left",
      minWidth = 110,
      filterable = TRUE
    ),
    stage_name = colDef(
      name = "Stage",
      minWidth = 540,
      filterable = TRUE,
      style = list(whiteSpace = "normal", lineHeight = "1.35")
    ),
    vote_report_type = colDef(
      name = "Vote report type",
      minWidth = 155,
      filterable = TRUE
    ),
    n_obs = colDef(
      name = "Rows per item",
      align = "right",
      minWidth = 130,
      format = colFormat(digits = 0)
    ),
    item_url = colDef(show = FALSE) # kept in data for the cell renderer above, hidden from display
  ),
  fullWidth = TRUE,
  compact = TRUE,
  highlight = FALSE,
  outlined = TRUE,
  searchable = TRUE,
  defaultPageSize = 10,
  defaultSorted = "n_obs",
  defaultSortOrder = "desc",
  theme = compact_table_theme
) %>%
  style_reactable_table(
    "ITEMS WITH DUPLICATE VOTE ROWS IN A STAGE",
    paste0(
      "Items with more than one vote row for the same stage (committee, second or third reading). Data as of ",
      data_cutoff,
      "."
    )
  )
Show items with duplicate vote rows in a stage

ITEMS WITH DUPLICATE VOTE ROWS IN A STAGE

Items with more than one vote row for the same stage (committee, second or third reading). Data as of 2026-08-06.

Source: www.parlament.gv.at. Analysis: Roland Schmidt - @zoowalk.bsky.social - https://werk.statt.codes

As it turns out, some are duplicates in the data source — see for instance XX/I/1530, where the votes in the second and third reading are simply reported twice. Others appear multiple times because an item was partly approved and partly rejected within one single reading, and hence got two rows in the data source, as in XXVIII/I/403.

Rather than trying to repair these inconsistencies one by one, I simply remove the affected items from the analysis. Subsequently, I narrow the data down to items with a ‘regular’ vote report. A second duplicate check follows the type filter — it is purely defensive and in practice finds nothing, since taking a subset of rows cannot create a duplicate that wasn’t already there — but it makes the invariant explicit rather than assumed. The last line below shows which share of the original vote stages survives all these filters.

Remove items with duplicate stage rows, keep regular vote type only 
# drop items that had duplicate rows within a stage; only clean items remain
items_scope_pairs <- items_scope %>%
  anti_join(., dup_rows, by = c("legis_period", "item_url"))
nrow(items_scope_pairs)
## [1] 7745

# sanity check: no item should now have more than one row per stage
items_scope_pairs %>%
  count(legis_period, item_url, reading, name = "n_rows") %>%
  filter(n_rows > 1) %>%
  nrow()
## [1] 0

table(items_scope_pairs$reading)
## 
##      committee         second second & third          third 
##           2562           2586              8           2589

# this analysis focuses only on "regular" votes (explicit Dafür/Dagegen party lists)
items_scope_pairs_regular <- items_scope_pairs %>%
  filter(vote_report_type == "regular")

# defensive re-check after the type filter. A row subset of an already-unique table cannot
# contain new duplicates, so this is expected to be empty — assert that rather than silently
# anti_join()ing against nothing, which would hide it if the invariant ever did break
dup_rows2 <- items_scope_pairs_regular %>%
  count(legis_period, item_url, reading, name = "n_rows") %>%
  filter(n_rows > 1)

stopifnot(nrow(dup_rows2) == 0)

nrow(items_scope_pairs_regular) # vote rows left after keeping only "regular" reports
## [1] 6783
nrow(items_scope_pairs_regular) / nrow(items_scope) # share of all vote stages covered
## [1] 0.8705082

3.4 Extract votes

Now to the heart of the matter: getting each party’s position out of the stage description. The text follows (mostly) the pattern ‘Dafür: party A, party B, dagegen: party C’, so the function below splits the string at the ‘dagegen’ boundary and cleans up both sides. Two details are worth mentioning: first, I keep only tokens which appear in a predefined list of valid party labels — this guards against vote counts, footnotes and other non-party fragments sneaking into the results. Second, since party labels changed over the legislative periods (e.g. the FPÖ appearing as ‘F’ in earlier periods), a small helper maps the historical variants onto one canonical name per party.

Define party normalisation and Dafür/Dagegen vote text parser 
# includes historical aliases (F, NEOS-LIF, F-BZÖ, S/V/N/G single-letter forms)
# alongside canonical modern names; used as an allowlist to filter out non-party tokens
valid_parties <- c(
  "SPÖ",
  "ÖVP",
  "F",
  "FPÖ",
  "GRÜNE",
  "L",
  "BZÖ",
  "STRONACH",
  "NEOS",
  "NEOS-LIF",
  "F-BZÖ",
  "JETZT",
  "PILZ",
  "NEOS/NEOS-LIF",
  "JETZT/PILZ",
  "S",
  "V",
  "N",
  "G",
  "T", # Team Stronach, single-letter form
  "J", # JETZT, single-letter form
  "B" # BZÖ, single-letter form
)

# maps historical/transitional party labels to a single canonical name per party
normalise_party <- function(party) {
  case_when(
    party %in% c("NEOS-LIF", "NEOS/NEOS-LIF") ~ "NEOS",
    party %in% c("JETZT", "PILZ", "JETZT/PILZ", "J") ~ "JETZT/PILZ",
    party == "F" ~ "FPÖ",
    party %in% c("F-BZÖ", "B") ~ "BZÖ",
    party == "S" ~ "SPÖ",
    party == "V" ~ "ÖVP",
    party == "N" ~ "NEOS",
    party == "G" ~ "GRÜNE",
    party == "T" ~ "STRONACH",
    TRUE ~ party
  )
}

fn_get_votes <- function(vt) {
  # inner helper: splits a raw comma-separated party string into a clean character vector
  clean_parties <- function(x) {
    if (is.na(x) || str_trim(x) == "-") {
      return(character(0))
    }

    x |>
      str_split(",\\s*") |>
      unlist() |>
      str_trim() |>
      # drop any parenthetical qualifier and keep the party label in front of it, e.g.
      # "SPÖ (Mehrheit)" -> "SPÖ", "GRÜNE (G tw." -> "GRÜNE", "BZÖ ( dafür Andere" -> "BZÖ".
      # This must strip from the opening paren: removing only a trailing ")" would leave
      # "SPÖ (Mehrheit", which fails the all-caps test below and silently loses the party.
      str_remove("\\s*\\(.*$") |>
      str_remove("\\)+$") |> # stray closing paren with no opener in this token
      str_trim() |>
      # keep only all-caps tokens (party abbreviations); drops vote counts, notes, etc.
      keep(\(p) {
        str_detect(
          p,
          regex("^[[:upper:]ÄÖÜ]+(?:[-/][[:upper:]ÄÖÜ]+)*$")
        )
      }) |>
      keep(\(p) p %in% valid_parties) # final guard against unknown tokens
  }

  # some stage texts use ". Dagegen:" (period separator) instead of ", dagegen:"
  # normalise to a consistent comma form so the split below works in both cases
  vt_norm <- str_replace(
    vt,
    regex("\\.\\s*Dagegen:", ignore_case = TRUE),
    ", dagegen:"
  )

  # split at the dagegen boundary; n=2 prevents splitting inside party lists
  parts <- str_split(
    vt_norm,
    regex(",\\s*dagegen:", ignore_case = TRUE),
    n = 2
  )[[1]]

  if (length(parts) != 2) {
    stop("Regular vote text does not contain both Dafür and Dagegen parts.")
  }

  if (!str_detect(parts[1], regex("Dafür:", ignore_case = TRUE))) {
    stop("Regular vote text does not contain a Dafür part.")
  }

  # strip the "Dafür:" label and everything before it (dotall handles multi-line stage names)
  yes_raw <- parts[1] |>
    str_remove(regex("^.*Dafür:\\s*", dotall = TRUE, ignore_case = TRUE))

  # parts[2] runs to the end of the string, so a *second* Dafür:/Dagegen: pair — e.g.
  # "dagegen: F (f dafür: Dr. Ofner)" — would otherwise leak that vote's parties into the
  # no-list once the parenthetical strip above keeps the leading token. Cut at that boundary.
  no_raw <- parts[2] |>
    str_remove(regex(
      "\\s*[.;]?\\s*(dafür|dagegen)\\s*:.*$",
      dotall = TRUE,
      ignore_case = TRUE
    ))

  list(
    vote_yes = clean_parties(yes_raw),
    vote_no = clean_parties(no_raw)
  )
}

With the function defined, applying it to the data is a one-liner. The result is a list column containing, for every vote stage, the vector of parties in favor and the vector of parties against.

Apply vote parser to extract yes/no party lists per stage 
# parse each stage_name string into a list(vote_yes, vote_no) of party vectors
items_scope_pairs_regular <- items_scope_pairs_regular %>%
  mutate(votes_li = map(stage_name, fn_get_votes))

The list column is handy, but for the actual analysis a ‘long’ data frame is more convenient: one row per item, reading, and party, with two indicator columns recording whether the party voted in favor and/or against. The summarise() at the end collapses any remaining duplicate rows.

Expand to one row per party per stage (long format) 
items_scope_pairs_regular_long <- items_scope_pairs_regular %>%
  mutate(
    votes_party = map(votes_li, \(v) {
      yes_parties <- normalise_party(v$vote_yes)
      no_parties <- normalise_party(v$vote_no)

      # union ensures each party appears once per stage even if somehow listed in both sides
      tibble(
        party = union(yes_parties, no_parties),
        yes = as.integer(party %in% yes_parties),
        no = as.integer(party %in% no_parties)
      )
    })
  ) %>%
  unnest(votes_party) %>%
  select(
    item_url,
    legis_period,
    type_doc,
    title,
    item_number,
    status_number,
    status_description,
    stage_date,
    stage_name,
    reading,
    vote_report_type,
    party,
    yes,
    no
  ) %>%
  group_by(across(-c(yes, no))) %>%
  # collapse duplicate rows (e.g. from deduplication edge cases) by taking the maximum vote value
  summarise(
    yes = max(yes, na.rm = TRUE),
    no = max(no, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

To detect flips between stages, we need each stage side by side. Hence, let’s pivot the long data frame into a wide format where each row is one item-party combination, with separate columns for the committee, second-reading and third-reading vote (yes_committee, no_committee, yes_second, no_second, yes_third, no_third). An NA in these columns means the party has no usable recorded position at that stage — either because it appears in neither the Dafür nor the Dagegen list, or because the stage text is one of the formats the parser can’t resolve into a party-level position.

The pivot also drops the handful of rows labelled second & third, where the source reports both readings as a single combined entry. Those can’t be assigned to one reading or the other, so they can’t contribute to a transition. Worth flagging alongside two earlier exclusions in the same spirit: stages whose description carries no vote-outcome text at all, and committee votes recorded only as einstimmig (‘unanimously’) — the latter tells us the outcome but names no parties, so no individual position can be read from it. Each of these removes real votes from the analysis; none of them is random, and all of them narrow the post to “votes where the record actually names who stood where”.

Pivot to wide format with separate committee/second/third columns 
items_scope_pairs_regular_wide <- items_scope_pairs_regular_long %>%
  # drop "second & third" combined rows; keep committee + clean individual readings
  # (vote_report_type is already restricted to "regular" upstream)
  filter(reading %in% c("committee", "second", "third")) %>%
  select(
    item_url,
    legis_period,
    type_doc,
    title,
    item_number,
    status_number,
    status_description,
    party,
    reading,
    vote_report_type,
    yes,
    no
  ) %>%
  # pivot so each row is one item × party with one yes_/no_ column per stage
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(
      item_url,
      legis_period,
      type_doc,
      title,
      item_number,
      status_number,
      status_description,
      party
    ),
    names_from = reading,
    values_from = c(vote_report_type, yes, no),
    names_glue = "{.value}_{reading}",
    # NA fills indicate the party has no recorded vote for that particular reading
    values_fill = list(
      vote_report_type = NA_character_,
      yes = NA_integer_,
      no = NA_integer_
    )
  )

Speaking of NAs — before drawing any conclusions, it’s worth checking how much missingness we are actually dealing with, and whether it is concentrated in particular legislative periods. The naniar package makes this a quick exercise.

Visualise missing values by legislative period 
# faceting by legis_period reveals whether missingness is period-specific or systemic
items_scope_pairs_regular_wide %>%
  naniar::vis_miss(facet = legis_period)

4 Results

Where along an item’s journey does a party actually change its mind — between the committee vote and the second reading, or between the second and the third reading? This is where the accommodation of opposition parties should become visible: if a governing majority makes concessions to win broader support, the resulting position changes should cluster at a particular stage. Below I prepare a tidy table of every transition and then work through it in five steps: the number of flips by legislative period and direction; where flips concentrate by party, first as absolute counts, then as each party’s share of its period’s movement, and then measured against the bills each party could actually have moved on; and a compact summary of which stage carries most of the movement. A final section leaves the aggregates behind and lists the individual bills where a position actually changed.

One structural point to keep in mind throughout, because it shapes the central result before any data is involved: the second and third readings of a bill are normally taken in the same sitting, minutes apart, whereas the committee vote happens days or weeks earlier, in a different room, with time for negotiation in between. So the two transitions are not comparable windows of opportunity. If it turns out that almost nothing moves between the second and third reading, that is in large part mechanical — there is barely any interval in which a position could change — and not evidence that parliamentary debate never persuades anyone. Read the committee → second reading step as “what happened between committee and the floor”, and the second → third step as “what happened during a single sitting”.

A note on denominators, since the charts below use more than one. Counts are counts — the first chart simply reports how many changes occurred, which makes periods with more (or more contested) bills look busier for that reason alone. Where a percentage is shown, it is a composition rather than a rate: the party tiles divide that period’s own position changes between the parties and add up to 100% within a column. That answers “who moved”, not “how often a party moves” — a party with a large share may have moved once in a quiet period. The stage × period tile at the end is the one genuine rate, dividing flips by all comparable pairs.

That leaves one thing the descriptive charts cannot tell you. A party that already voted yes at the earlier stage cannot flip no → yes — it was never in a position to make that move, so its absence from the counts is not evidence of immobility. Measuring movement against opportunity needs a denominator built from the position each party actually went in with, which is what the fourth chart does: it divides each party’s changes by the bills it went into holding the prior position, separately for every party and period. The stage × period tile at the end is a coarser rate that does not condition this way, and reads accordingly.

And a note on who counts as government: coalition membership is coded once per legislative period, which is an approximation. It is a poor one for GP XXVI in particular — that period covers the ÖVP-FPÖ coalition, its collapse after the Ibiza affair in May 2019, the subsequent ÖVP-only cabinet and the Bierlein caretaker government. Votes from the second half of GP XXVI are therefore labelled against a coalition that no longer existed, so the government/opposition split shown for that period should be read with care.

GP XXII carries a milder version of the same problem: the FPÖ split in 2005 and its ministers continued in government as the BZÖ, so both are coded as governing for the whole period. That is why the coalition label on the axis of the stage × period chart further below reads ‘ÖVP, FPÖ, BZÖ’ for that one period — an artefact of period-level coding, not a three-party coalition.

Build shared party/period/government lookups, then encode positions per stage and classify each transition’s change 
# hand-coded coalition membership per legislative period (GP XX–XXVIII)
gov_parties_lookup <- tribble(
  ~legis_period , ~party ,
  "XX"          , "SPÖ"  , "XX"     , "ÖVP"   ,
  "XXI"         , "ÖVP"  , "XXI"    , "F"     ,
  "XXII"        , "ÖVP"  , "XXII"   , "F"     , "XXII"   , "F-BZÖ" ,
  "XXIII"       , "SPÖ"  , "XXIII"  , "ÖVP"   ,
  "XXIV"        , "SPÖ"  , "XXIV"   , "ÖVP"   ,
  "XXV"         , "SPÖ"  , "XXV"    , "ÖVP"   ,
  "XXVI"        , "ÖVP"  , "XXVI"   , "FPÖ"   ,
  "XXVII"       , "ÖVP"  , "XXVII"  , "GRÜNE" ,
  "XXVIII"      , "ÖVP"  , "XXVIII" , "SPÖ"   , "XXVIII" , "NEOS"
) %>%
  mutate(party = normalise_party(party)) %>% # align aliases before joining
  mutate(is_gov = TRUE)

all_periods_vec <- c(
  "XX",
  "XXI",
  "XXII",
  "XXIII",
  "XXIV",
  "XXV",
  "XXVI",
  "XXVII",
  "XXVIII"
)

# tracks which party × period combinations actually appear in the data
# used later to distinguish "not in parliament" (white) from "zero flips" (grey)
party_period_presence <- items_scope_pairs_regular_wide %>%
  distinct(legis_period, party) %>%
  mutate(present = TRUE)

all_parties <- union(party_period_presence$party, gov_parties_lookup$party)

# fixed top order, then remaining parties by presence across legislative periods
party_order_priority <- c("FPÖ", "ÖVP", "SPÖ", "GRÜNE", "NEOS")

party_order <- c(
  party_order_priority,
  party_period_presence %>%
    distinct(party, legis_period) %>%
    count(party, name = "periods_present") %>%
    right_join(tibble(party = all_parties), by = "party") %>%
    mutate(periods_present = replace_na(periods_present, 0L)) %>%
    filter(!party %in% party_order_priority) %>%
    arrange(desc(periods_present), party) %>%
    pull(party)
) %>%
  unique()

# position held by each party at each stage (NA = no recorded vote at that stage)
stage_positions <- items_scope_pairs_regular_wide %>%
  mutate(
    pos_committee = case_when(
      yes_committee == 1 ~ "Dafür",
      no_committee == 1 ~ "Dagegen",
      .default = NA_character_
    ),
    pos_second = case_when(
      yes_second == 1 ~ "Dafür",
      no_second == 1 ~ "Dagegen",
      .default = NA_character_
    ),
    pos_third = case_when(
      yes_third == 1 ~ "Dafür",
      no_third == 1 ~ "Dagegen",
      .default = NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    gov_parties_lookup %>% select(legis_period, party, is_gov),
    by = c("legis_period", "party")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    role = factor(
      if_else(replace_na(is_gov, FALSE), "Government", "Opposition"),
      levels = c("Government", "Opposition")
    )
  )

# one row per party × item × transition, keeping the position held BEFORE and after.
# from_pos records the position a party went in with, i.e. which changes it was in a
# position to make: a prior 'no' is the only thing that can become a 'no → yes'. The
# conditional chart further below uses exactly this to build its denominators.
transitions <- bind_rows(
  stage_positions %>%
    transmute(
      item_url,
      legis_period,
      type_doc,
      party,
      role,
      transition = "Committee → 2nd reading",
      from_pos = pos_committee,
      to_pos = pos_second
    ),
  stage_positions %>%
    transmute(
      item_url,
      legis_period,
      type_doc,
      party,
      role,
      transition = "2nd → 3rd reading",
      from_pos = pos_second,
      to_pos = pos_third
    )
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(from_pos), !is.na(to_pos)) %>% # observed at both stages of the step
  mutate(
    change = case_when(
      from_pos == to_pos ~ "no change",
      from_pos == "Dagegen" & to_pos == "Dafür" ~ "no → yes",
      from_pos == "Dafür" & to_pos == "Dagegen" ~ "yes → no"
    ),
    transition = factor(
      transition,
      levels = c("Committee → 2nd reading", "2nd → 3rd reading")
    )
  )

# how many comparable pairs and how many flips at each transition?
transitions %>% count(transition, change) %>% print(n = Inf)
## # A tibble: 6 × 3
##   transition              change        n
##   <fct>                   <chr>     <int>
## 1 Committee → 2nd reading no change  8728
## 2 Committee → 2nd reading no → yes    246
## 3 Committee → 2nd reading yes → no    108
## 4 2nd → 3rd reading       no change  9665
## 5 2nd → 3rd reading       no → yes     22
## 6 2nd → 3rd reading       yes → no      8
transitions %>% count(transition, name = "eligible_pairs")
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
##   transition              eligible_pairs
##   <fct>                            <int>
## 1 Committee → 2nd reading           9082
## 2 2nd → 3rd reading                 9695

# concise caption for the exploratory charts below
# (the full item-list caption is too tall for these denser, multi-facet plots)
vote_graph_caption_short <- paste0(
  "Data: www&#46;parlament.gv.at via ParlAT package, as of ",
  data_cutoff,
  " · Graphic: Roland Schmidt, https&#58;//werk.statt.codes · NR government bills (Regierungsvorlagen) only, regular votes only (GP XX–XXVIII)"
)

4.1 Flip counts by period and direction

The most direct answer. For each legislative period, the bars compare the number of position changes at the two transitions, split into the two directions (no → yes, a move toward support; yes → no, a withdrawal).

The chart covers opposition parties only. Government parties are left out deliberately: across all nine periods there is exactly one government-party flip in the data, on three comparable pairs, so a rate for them is built on too little to plot and an absolute bar for them would be a single unit high. That near-total absence is itself worth stating — a party does not usually vote against the bill its own government tabled — but it is a sentence, not a panel.

It’s worth being precise about what a tall bar means, because the intuitive reading is the wrong way round. A flip at committee → 2nd reading means a party voted one way in committee and differently on the floor — so the position moved in the interval between the two, once the committee stage was already over. A deal actually struck inside the committee produces the opposite: the party votes yes there and yes again later, and contributes no flip at all. So tall left-hand (committee → 2nd) bars say that positions were still moving after the committee had reported; tall right-hand (2nd → 3rd) bars would say they moved during the plenary sitting itself.

Because these are counts rather than rates, they are not normalised for how much each period had on the table: a period with more bills, or more contested ones, has more opportunities to flip. The normalised view comes further below, in the share-of-comparable-bills heatmap.

Per-period bars: flip counts by transition and direction, opposition parties 
# opposition only: government parties contribute a single flip across all nine periods
flip_dirs <- transitions %>%
  filter(role == "Opposition", change %in% c("no → yes", "yes → no")) %>%
  count(legis_period, transition, change, name = "n_flip") %>%
  # complete the grid so a measured zero is visible as "0" rather than as a missing bar
  complete(
    legis_period = all_periods_vec,
    transition,
    change,
    fill = list(n_flip = 0L)
  ) %>%
  mutate(legis_period = factor(legis_period, levels = all_periods_vec))

p_where_bars <- flip_dirs %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = legis_period, y = n_flip, fill = transition)) +
  geom_col(
    # bar width and dodge width must agree, otherwise the count labels below are
    # positioned on a different grid than the bars they annotate
    position = position_dodge2(width = 0.9, preserve = "single"),
    width = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = n_flip),
    position = position_dodge2(width = 0.9, preserve = "single"),
    vjust = -0.3,
    size = 2.5,
    family = "Noto Sans",
    colour = "grey35"
  ) +
  facet_grid(change ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Committee → 2nd reading" = "#4575b4",
      "2nd → 3rd reading" = "#fdae61"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of position changes",
    title = "Where do parties change their position?",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Number of position changes at each transition — committee → 2nd reading (blue) vs ",
      "2nd → 3rd reading (orange) — by direction, opposition parties only. ",
      "A high committee → 2nd bar means positions were still moving between the committee ",
      "vote and the plenary; a high 2nd → 3rd bar means they moved during the sitting itself.<br>",
      "<span style='font-size:9pt;color:grey40;'>Counts are not normalised for how many comparable bills each period had, so periods are not directly comparable here. NR, regular votes only, GP XX–XXVIII.</span>"
    ),
    caption = vote_graph_caption_short
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11, base_family = "Noto Sans") +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 14,
      margin = ggplot2::margin(b = 4)
    ),
    plot.subtitle = ggtext::element_textbox_simple(
      size = 10,
      colour = "grey30",
      lineheight = 1.3,
      margin = ggplot2::margin(b = 10)
    ),
    plot.caption = ggtext::element_textbox_simple(
      size = 8,
      colour = "grey45",
      margin = ggplot2::margin(t = 10)
    ),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10)
  )

p_where_bars

4.2 Flip counts and shares by party

A party × period tile grid, faceted by transition (rows) and direction (columns), so each party–period cell appears four times — once for each combination of the two transitions (committee → 2nd, 2nd → 3rd) and the two directions (no → yes, yes → no). Counts, not rates, so it reads as “how many flips, and at which step”. Government parties carry a thick black frame.

Tile heatmap of flip counts faceted by transition and direction 
flip_tiles <- transitions %>%
  filter(change %in% c("no → yes", "yes → no")) %>%
  count(legis_period, party, transition, change, name = "n_flip")

# full party × period × transition × direction grid so empty cells render correctly
where_tile_grid <- expand_grid(
  party = all_parties,
  legis_period = all_periods_vec,
  transition = c("Committee → 2nd reading", "2nd → 3rd reading"),
  change = c("no → yes", "yes → no")
) %>%
  left_join(
    flip_tiles %>% mutate(transition = as.character(transition)),
    by = c("party", "legis_period", "transition", "change")
  ) %>%
  replace_na(list(n_flip = 0)) %>%
  left_join(gov_parties_lookup, by = c("party", "legis_period")) %>%
  replace_na(list(is_gov = FALSE)) %>%
  left_join(party_period_presence, by = c("party", "legis_period")) %>%
  replace_na(list(present = FALSE)) %>%
  mutate(
    party = factor(party, levels = rev(party_order)),
    legis_period = factor(legis_period, levels = all_periods_vec),
    transition = factor(
      transition,
      levels = c("Committee → 2nd reading", "2nd → 3rd reading")
    ),
    label = if_else(n_flip > 0, as.character(n_flip), ""),
    fill_val = if_else(present, as.numeric(n_flip), NA_real_),
    # negate yes-to-no counts so a single diverging scale can colour the two
    # direction facets differently (red = yes -> no, green = no -> yes)
    fill_val_signed = if_else(change == "yes → no", -fill_val, fill_val)
  )

n_max_where <- max(1, max(where_tile_grid$n_flip, na.rm = TRUE))

# the diverging scale passes through near-white at its midpoint, so small counts sit on a
# pale tile — white digits would be invisible there. Same approach as the percent heatmap.
where_tile_grid <- where_tile_grid %>%
  mutate(label_colour = if_else(n_flip > n_max_where / 2, "white", "grey15"))

p_where_heatmap <- where_tile_grid %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = legis_period, y = party, fill = fill_val_signed)) +
  geom_tile(
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_tile(
    data = where_tile_grid %>% filter(is_gov),
    aes(x = legis_period, y = party),
    fill = NA,
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 0.4,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = where_tile_grid %>% filter(n_flip > 0, present),
    mapping = aes(
      x = legis_period,
      y = party,
      label = label,
      colour = label_colour
    ),
    size = 2.8,
    fontface = "bold",
    family = "Noto Sans",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  # switch = "y" moves the transition strip from the right edge to the left
  facet_grid(transition ~ change, switch = "y") +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#b2182b",
    mid = "grey92",
    high = "#1a9850",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-n_max_where, n_max_where),
    na.value = "white",
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    title = "Flip counts by party, period, transition and direction",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Columns: direction (red = yes → no, green = no → yes). Rows: where the flip occurs (committee → 2nd vs 2nd → 3rd). ",
      "Colour intensity = number of flips; white = party not represented; thick black frame = governing party.<br>",
      "<span style='font-size:9pt;color:grey40;'>NR, regular votes only, GP XX–XXVIII.</span>"
    ),
    caption = vote_graph_caption_short
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11, base_family = "Noto Sans") +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 14,
      margin = ggplot2::margin(b = 4)
    ),
    plot.subtitle = ggtext::element_textbox_simple(
      size = 10,
      colour = "grey30",
      lineheight = 1.3,
      margin = ggplot2::margin(b = 10)
    ),
    plot.caption = ggtext::element_textbox_simple(
      size = 8,
      colour = "grey45",
      margin = ggplot2::margin(t = 10)
    ),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    strip.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10, hjust = 0),
    # place the switched y strip outside the party labels rather than between
    # them and the panel
    strip.placement = "outside",
    strip.text.y.left = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10, angle = 90)
  )

p_where_heatmap

4.3 Who accounts for the movement in each period?

The counts above say how much movement there was; they don’t say how it was distributed between the parties. The chart below answers that by turning each legislative period into a composition: within one period, one transition and one direction, the tiles give each party’s share of that period’s position changes and sum to 100%.

So a tile reads as “of everything that moved in this period, this party accounted for X% of it”. That makes the balance between parties in a given period directly readable down a column — which the raw counts obscure whenever one period simply produced more movement than another.

Two cautions. A share says nothing about volume: a party can hold 100% of a period’s flips because it was the only one that moved, on a single bill. Read the tiles together with the counts chart above, which supplies the magnitudes. And because each column is normalised on its own, shares are not comparable across periods — only within one.

Tile heatmap: each party’s share of its period’s position changes 
# count unique bills on which each party flips in each direction
flip_bill_counts <- transitions %>%
  filter(change %in% c("no → yes", "yes → no")) %>%
  group_by(legis_period, party, transition, change) %>%
  summarise(n_flip_bills = n_distinct(item_url), .groups = "drop")

# reuse the absolute heatmap's complete grid, party order, presence and government flags
where_tile_rate_grid <- where_tile_grid %>%
  select(-n_flip, -label, -fill_val) %>%
  left_join(
    flip_bill_counts,
    by = c("legis_period", "party", "transition", "change")
  ) %>%
  replace_na(list(n_flip_bills = 0L)) %>%
  # the denominator is the period's own total, so each column is a composition:
  # the party shares within one period x transition x direction add up to 100%
  mutate(
    n_period_flips = sum(n_flip_bills),
    .by = c(legis_period, transition, change)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    party = factor(party, levels = levels(where_tile_grid$party)),
    legis_period = factor(legis_period, levels = all_periods_vec),
    transition = factor(
      transition,
      levels = c("Committee → 2nd reading", "2nd → 3rd reading")
    ),
    # a period with no movement at all has no composition to show, hence NA not 0/0
    rate = if_else(n_period_flips > 0, n_flip_bills / n_period_flips, NA_real_),
    label = if_else(
      present & n_flip_bills > 0,
      scales::percent(rate, accuracy = 1),
      ""
    ),
    fill_rate = if_else(present, rate, NA_real_),
    # negate yes-to-no rates so a single diverging scale can colour the two
    # direction facets differently (red = yes -> no, green = no -> yes)
    fill_rate_signed = if_else(change == "yes → no", -fill_rate, fill_rate)
  )

# The defining property of a composition: within one period x transition x direction the
# party shares must add up to exactly 1 wherever anything moved at all. Assert it rather
# than trust it — a stray join could silently inflate a denominator without changing a colour.
composition_check <- where_tile_rate_grid %>%
  filter(n_period_flips > 0) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(rate), .by = c(legis_period, transition, change))

stopifnot(
  all(abs(composition_check$total - 1) < 1e-9),
  all(
    where_tile_rate_grid$n_flip_bills <= where_tile_rate_grid$n_period_flips,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
)

rate_max_where <- max(where_tile_rate_grid$rate, na.rm = TRUE)

where_tile_rate_grid <- where_tile_rate_grid %>%
  mutate(
    label_colour = if_else(rate > rate_max_where / 2, "white", "grey15")
  )

p_where_heatmap_percent <- where_tile_rate_grid %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = legis_period, y = party, fill = fill_rate_signed)) +
  geom_tile(
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_tile(
    data = where_tile_rate_grid %>% filter(is_gov),
    aes(x = legis_period, y = party),
    fill = NA,
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 0.4,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = where_tile_rate_grid %>% filter(n_flip_bills > 0, present),
    mapping = aes(
      x = legis_period,
      y = party,
      label = label,
      colour = label_colour
    ),
    size = 2.8,
    fontface = "bold",
    family = "Noto Sans",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  # switch = "y" moves the transition strip from the right edge to the left
  facet_grid(transition ~ change, switch = "y") +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#b2182b",
    mid = "grey92",
    high = "#1a9850",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-rate_max_where, rate_max_where),
    na.value = "white",
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  labs(
    x = NULL,

    title = "Who accounts for each period's position changes?",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Each tile shows a party's share of all position changes recorded in that legislative ",
      "period, for that transition and direction (red = yes → no, green = no → yes). ",
      "**Within a column the shares add up to 100%**, so the tiles show how the movement of a ",
      "period was divided between the parties, not how often any one party moved. ",
      "A share is not a volume: 100% can mean a single flip that no other party matched — read ",
      "alongside the counts above. ",
      "White = party not represented; grey = no flips; thick black frame = governing party.<br>",
      "<span style='font-size:9pt;color:grey40;'>Shares are normalised within each period, so they are comparable down a column but not across periods. NR, regular votes only, GP XX–XXVIII.</span>"
    ),
    caption = vote_graph_caption_short
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11, base_family = "Noto Sans") +

4.4 Both numbers at once

The two charts above each hide what the other shows. The counts say how much moved but not how it was divided; the shares say how it was divided but not how much there was to divide — which is why a single flip can render as a confident 100%.

The chart below prints both in the same cell: the count on top, that party’s share of the period underneath, with a Period total row carrying the column’s own total and the 100% it sums to. Where a share looks dramatic, the count immediately above it says how much weight to give it — a 100% sitting on a 1 is one bill, not a pattern.

Tile heatmap combining absolute counts and within-period shares 
# One summary row per panel column, carrying the column's own total. fill_rate_signed is NA so
# the row picks up the scale's neutral na.value and reads as a header rather than as the
# darkest tile on the chart.
period_totals <- where_tile_rate_grid %>%
  distinct(legis_period, transition, change, n_period_flips) %>%
  mutate(
    party = "Period total",
    n_flip_bills = n_period_flips,
    rate = if_else(n_period_flips > 0, 1, NA_real_),
    present = TRUE,
    is_gov = FALSE,
    fill_rate_signed = NA_real_
  )

where_tile_combined <- where_tile_rate_grid %>%
  bind_rows(period_totals) %>%
  mutate(
    # "Period total" goes last so it renders at the TOP of each panel
    party = factor(party, levels = c(rev(party_order), "Period total")),
    is_total = party == "Period total",
    label_n = if_else(present & n_flip_bills > 0, as.character(n_flip_bills), ""),
    # a period with no movement has no composition, so print no percentage rather than "100%"
    label_pct = if_else(
      present & n_flip_bills > 0 & !is.na(rate),
      scales::percent(rate, accuracy = 1),
      ""
    ),
    # totals sit on the neutral header tile, so they always take the dark ink
    label_colour = if_else(
      is_total,
      "grey15",
      if_else(!is.na(rate) & rate > rate_max_where / 2, "white", "grey15")
    )
  )

4.5 How often did a party move when it actually could?

Everything so far counts changes. But a count alone can mislead in a specific way: a party can only flip no → yes on a bill it went into holding no. If it already voted yes in committee, that bill was never available to it, and its absence from the flip counts says nothing about how willing it was to be won over. A party that agrees with the government most of the time will look immobile in the counts for a reason that has nothing to do with mobility.

So this section conditions on what was actually available. For each party, in each legislative period and at each transition, the bar height is the number of bills the party went into holding the prior position — the ones it could have moved on. The coloured segment is the subset it did move on. The proportion of the bar that is coloured is the conditional rate, and because the bar keeps its full height, you can see at once whether a high rate rests on forty bills or on two.

Two things to keep in mind. Each row has its own y-scale, because party volumes differ by an order of magnitude — bar heights are therefore not comparable between parties, only the coloured proportions and each party’s own trajectory. And the 2nd → 3rd reading columns are nearly empty throughout: only about thirty changes occur there across all nine periods, which is the same same-sitting artefact discussed earlier, not a finding about those parties.

Segmented bars: bills available to flip, and the share actually flipped 
# Condition on what was available: `direction` is the move the party's prior position made
# possible (a prior "no" can only become a "no → yes"), and `flipped` says whether it happened.
# `transitions` is already restricted to pairs observed at both stages, so counting it directly
# gives the denominator -- the bills the party actually went into holding that position.
conditional_flips <- transitions %>%
  mutate(
    direction = if_else(from_pos == "Dagegen", "no → yes", "yes → no"),
    flipped = change %in% c("no → yes", "yes → no")
  ) %>%
  count(legis_period, party, transition, direction, flipped, name = "n") %>%
  # keep only party x period combinations where the party actually held seats
  semi_join(party_period_presence, by = c("legis_period", "party")) %>%
  mutate(
    segment = case_when(
      !flipped ~ "held",
      direction == "no → yes" ~ "flipped_no_yes",
      .default = "flipped_yes_no"
    ) %>%
      factor(levels = c("held", "flipped_no_yes", "flipped_yes_no")),
    party = factor(party, levels = party_order),
    legis_period = factor(legis_period, levels = all_periods_vec),
    transition = factor(
      transition,
      levels = c("Committee → 2nd reading", "2nd → 3rd reading")
    )
  )

# per-bar totals and the conditional rate, used for the labels above each bar
conditional_rates <- conditional_flips %>%
  summarise(
    n_available = sum(n),
    n_flipped = sum(n[flipped]),
    .by = c(legis_period, party, transition, direction)
  ) %>%
  mutate(rate = n_flipped / n_available)

# The flipped counts here must reconcile with the counts charts above: summed across parties,
# they are the same position changes. Assert it so the two cannot silently diverge.
reconcile_conditional <- conditional_rates %>%
  summarise(n_flipped = sum(n_flipped), .by = c(legis_period, transition, direction)) %>%
  inner_join(
    where_tile_rate_grid %>%
      distinct(legis_period, transition, change, n_period_flips) %>%
      mutate(legis_period = factor(legis_period, levels = all_periods_vec)),
    by = c("legis_period", "transition", "direction" = "change")
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(reconcile_conditional) > 0,
  all(reconcile_conditional$n_flipped == reconcile_conditional$n_period_flips)
)

p_conditional_bars <- conditional_flips %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = legis_period, y = n, fill = segment)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75) +
  geom_text(
    data = conditional_rates %>% filter(n_flipped > 0),
    mapping = aes(
      x = legis_period,
      y = n_available,
      label = scales::percent(rate, accuracy = 1)
    ),
    vjust = -0.35,
    size = 1.8,
    family = "Noto Sans",
    colour = "grey30",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_grid(party ~ transition + direction, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "held" = "grey85",
      "flipped_no_yes" = "#1a9850",
      "flipped_yes_no" = "#b2182b"
    ),
    labels = c(
      "held" = "Held its position",
      "flipped_no_yes" = "Changed to yes",
      "flipped_yes_no" = "Changed to no"
