  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Bills the party went into holding the prior position",
    title = "Movement measured against opportunity, not against everything",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Bar height = the bills a party went into holding the prior position, i.e. the ones it ",
      "**could** have changed its mind on. The coloured segment is the subset it actually did ",
      "change, and the percentage above each bar is that share. Keeping the full base visible ",
      "shows whether a rate rests on many bills or on two.<br>",
      "<span style='font-size:9pt;color:grey40;'>Each row has its own y-scale, so bar heights are not comparable between parties — only the coloured proportions and each party's own trajectory. NR, regular votes only, GP XX–XXVIII.</span>"
    ),
    caption = vote_graph_caption_short
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11, base_family = "Noto Sans") +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 7),

4.6 The headline pattern: stage × period

The most compact summary of all: a single tile grid with the two transitions on the x-axis and the legislative periods down the y-axis. Each tile’s colour is the relative number of flips — the share of comparable party–item pairs that change position at that transition — with the absolute count combining both directions. It makes the headline pattern unmissable: the committee → 2nd reading column is consistently darker than the 2nd → 3rd column.

Heatmap of relative flip rate by stage and legislative period 
flip_stage_period <- transitions %>%
  group_by(legis_period, transition) %>%
  summarise(
    eligible = n(),
    n_flip = sum(change %in% c("no → yes", "yes → no")),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    rate = n_flip / eligible,
    legis_period = factor(legis_period, levels = rev(all_periods_vec)),
    # white text on dark tiles, dark text on light tiles
    lab_colour = if_else(rate > max(rate) / 2, "white", "grey15")
  )

gov_axis_labels <- gov_parties_lookup %>%
  group_by(legis_period) %>%
  summarise(
    gov_parties = paste(party, collapse = ", "),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  tibble::deframe()

# every period on the axis must have a coalition label, otherwise the static vector built
# below would silently pair periods with the wrong government
stopifnot(all(all_periods_vec %in% names(gov_axis_labels)))

# Build the secondary-axis labels as an explicit, name-matched vector in the same order as
# the y-axis levels (which are reversed, so the newest period sits on top). Deriving them
# inside the labeller from the values ggplot passes in is fragile: on a discrete scale it
# receives integer positions rather than level names, so the lookup would be positional and
# would break silently if a period were missing or the level order changed.
gov_axis_labels_ordered <- unname(gov_axis_labels[rev(all_periods_vec)])

p_flip_stage_period <- flip_stage_period %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = transition, y = legis_period, fill = rate)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = scales::percent(rate, accuracy = 0.1), colour = lab_colour),
    family = "Noto Sans",
    size = 3.3
  ) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "grey94",
    high = "#3b0f70",
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
    name = "Flip rate"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  scale_y_discrete(
    breaks = levels(flip_stage_period$legis_period),
    sec.axis = dup_axis(
      labels = gov_axis_labels_ordered,
      name = NULL
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    title = "Relative number of flips by stage and legislative period",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Tile colour = share of comparable party–item pairs that change position at each transition ",
      "(both directions combined, all parties). The committee → 2nd reading step carries almost all of the movement.<br>",
      "<span style='font-size:9pt;color:grey40;'>NR, regular votes only.</span>"
    ),
    caption = vote_graph_caption_short
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11, base_family = "Noto Sans") +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y.right = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"),
    axis.title.y.right = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right",

4.7 A closer look: items decided at all three stages

Now that committee votes come from the reports, the full committee → 2nd → 3rd path is observable for most bills, not just a contested few. This section narrows to exactly those items — the ones with a recorded regular vote at the committee, the second reading and the third reading — so we can trace each party’s position across all three stages and see where, if anywhere, it changes.

The condition is applied per item, not per party: it guarantees that all three stages carry a vote row, not that every party appears in all three of them. A party absent from both the Dafür and the Dagegen list at one stage still has no position there, which is why the change flags below propagate NA rather than assuming continuity.

Restrict to items with a recorded vote at committee, 2nd and 3rd reading 
# positions per item × party × stage (NA where the party has no vote at that stage)
three_stage_long <- items_scope_pairs_regular_long %>%
  filter(reading %in% c("committee", "second", "third")) %>%
  mutate(
    pos = case_when(
      yes == 1 ~ "Dafür",
      no == 1 ~ "Dagegen",
      .default = NA_character_
    )
  )

# keep only items that carry a recorded vote at ALL three stages
three_stage_items <- three_stage_long %>%
  distinct(item_url, reading) %>%
  count(item_url, name = "n_stages") %>%
  filter(n_stages == 3)

# one row per item × party, positions and dates of the three stages side by side
three_stage_wide <- three_stage_long %>%
  semi_join(three_stage_items, by = "item_url") %>%
  select(legis_period, item_url, title, party, reading, pos, stage_date) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = reading, values_from = c(pos, stage_date)) %>%
  left_join(
    gov_parties_lookup %>% select(legis_period, party, is_gov),
    by = c("legis_period", "party")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    role = if_else(replace_na(is_gov, FALSE), "Government", "Opposition"),
    change_committee_2nd = pos_committee != pos_second, # NA if a stage is missing
    change_2nd_3rd = pos_second != pos_third
  )

cat(
  "Items with a recorded vote at all three stages:",
  nrow(three_stage_items),
  "\n"
)
## Items with a recorded vote at all three stages: 1849
cat("Party–item rows in this subset:", nrow(three_stage_wide), "\n")
## Party–item rows in this subset: 9078
# where do the changes sit?
three_stage_wide %>%
  summarise(
    `committee → 2nd` = sum(change_committee_2nd, na.rm = TRUE),
    `2nd → 3rd` = sum(change_2nd_3rd, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  print()
## # A tibble: 1 × 2
##   `committee → 2nd` `2nd → 3rd`
##               <int>       <int>
## 1               350          27

Within this subset, virtually every recorded position change happens at the committee → second reading step; the second → third reading step almost never moves anyone. The table below lists every party–item change in the subset, most recent first, each linked to its source page so the individual case can be checked.

Table of every committee → 2nd → 3rd position change, most recent first 
three_stage_changes <- three_stage_wide %>%
  filter(change_committee_2nd | change_2nd_3rd) %>%
  mutate(
    where = case_when(
      replace_na(change_committee_2nd, FALSE) &
        replace_na(change_2nd_3rd, FALSE) ~ "committee → 2nd & 2nd → 3rd",
      replace_na(change_committee_2nd, FALSE) ~ "committee → 2nd",
      replace_na(change_2nd_3rd, FALSE) ~ "2nd → 3rd"
    ),
    item_ref = item_url %>%
      str_remove("^https://www\\.parlament\\.gv\\.at/gegenstand/") %>%
      str_remove("\\?.*$")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(stage_date_second)) %>%
  select(
    legis_period,
    item_ref,
    title,
    party,
    role,
    pos_committee,
    pos_second,
    pos_third,
    where,
    stage_date_second,
    item_url
  )

# shared colour styling for the three position columns
pos_style <- function(value) {
  if (is.na(value)) {
    return(list(color = "#bbb"))
  }
  list(
    color = if (value == "Dafür") "#1a7a3c" else "#c0392b",
    fontWeight = "600"
  )
}

three_stage_changes_table <- reactable(
  three_stage_changes,
  columns = list(
    legis_period = colDef(
      name = "GP",
      align = "right",
      minWidth = 60,
      filterable = TRUE
    ),
    item_ref = colDef(
      name = "Item",
      minWidth = 110,
      filterable = TRUE,
      cell = function(value, index) {
        htmltools::tags$a(
          href = three_stage_changes$item_url[index],
          target = "_blank",
          value
        )
      }
    ),
    title = colDef(
      name = "Title",
      minWidth = 240,
      filterable = TRUE,
      style = list(whiteSpace = "normal", lineHeight = "1.3")
    ),
    party = colDef(name = "Party", minWidth = 80, filterable = TRUE),
    role = colDef(name = "Role", minWidth = 110, filterable = TRUE),
    pos_committee = colDef(
      name = "Committee",
      minWidth = 95,
      style = pos_style
    ),
    pos_second = colDef(name = "2nd reading", minWidth = 95, style = pos_style),
    pos_third = colDef(name = "3rd reading", minWidth = 95, style = pos_style),
    where = colDef(name = "Change at", minWidth = 150, filterable = TRUE),
    stage_date_second = colDef(
      name = "2nd reading date",
      minWidth = 130,
      filterable = TRUE
    ),
    item_url = colDef(show = FALSE)
  ),
  fullWidth = TRUE,
  compact = TRUE,
  highlight = TRUE,
  outlined = TRUE,
  searchable = TRUE,
  defaultPageSize = 12,
  theme = compact_table_theme
) %>%
  style_reactable_table(
    "POSITION CHANGES AMONG ITEMS DECIDED AT ALL THREE STAGES",
    paste0(
      "Every party–item whose position differs between two consecutive stages, sorted by second-reading date, most recent first. Data as of ",
      data_cutoff,
      "."
    )
  )

The most recent item in this subset with a committee → second-reading change is Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Beschleunigungsgesetz, Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz, Änderung (XXVIII/I/449), voted on 2026-06-11. 5 Wrap-up

So, where does a party actually change its mind on a government bill? The short answer: between the committee and the floor, and almost nowhere else.

Across 2,710 Regierungsvorlagen from the 20th to the 28th legislative period, 3.90% of the comparable party–bill pairs change position between the committee vote and the second reading (354 of 9,082), against 0.31% between the second and the third reading (30 of 9,695). That is 92.2% of all the movement in the data sitting in one of the two steps. Taking the three questions from the top in turn:

Between which stages? Committee → second reading, overwhelmingly. But recall what that interval is and is not: the second and third readings are typically taken minutes apart in the same sitting, so the near-absence of movement there is substantially mechanical rather than a finding about plenary debate. The committee → second reading step is the one that actually contains days or weeks in which something could be negotiated — and it is the one where the changes show up.

Which parties? In the 1,849-bill subset observable at all three stages, changes are almost exclusively an opposition phenomenon: 359 of the 360 recorded changes come from opposition parties. GRÜNE accounts for the largest single share (135), followed by the other long-serving opposition parties. That asymmetry is the expected shape if these flips are the trace of a governing majority buying support rather than of parties independently reconsidering the merits — a government party has little reason to vote against its own bill in committee in the first place.

Under which government? Here I’d rather under-claim. The raw counts are highest in the earlier periods, but as flagged at the outset, legislative periods are not directly comparable: they differ in length, in how many bills they produced, and in how contested those bills were. A period with more no votes at the committee stage simply has more opportunities to flip. The per-period tiles show the pattern holding throughout, but I would not read the ranking between periods as a ranking of governmental responsiveness.

One direction is worth flagging on its own. At the committee → second reading step, moves toward support outnumber withdrawals by roughly 2.3 to 1 (246 versus 108). Positions converge on their way to the floor far more often than they fracture.

A closing caveat on what this does and does not show. These numbers locate where positions change; they cannot say why. A flip from no to yes is consistent with a concession having been made — that was the motivating hunch — but it is equally consistent with an opposition party simply being persuaded, or with the committee stage having clarified something the party had misread. Establishing the difference means reading the individual bill and what changed in it between the two votes. The table above links every case, so that check is at least available for anyone who wants to make it on a specific bill.

Finally, the scope: this post covers government bills only. Items initiated inside the National Council follow a different political logic, and whether the same pattern holds for them is a separate question — and a good candidate for a Part III.
